Do not stop for Maghrib on the way out of Arafah: when asked, the Prophet ﷺ said, "The prayer is ahead of you" (Bukhari {1}). On reaching Muzdalifah he prayed Maghrib and Isha together, with one adhan and two iqamahs and no voluntary prayer between them (Muslim {2}; Bukhari {3}, {4}). Maghrib stays three rakahs; Isha is shortened to two (four if your school counts you a resident of Makkah; in the relied-upon Shafi'i view such a resident also prays Maghrib and Isha each at its own time). If you fear you will arrive only after midnight, many scholars (including the Saudi fatwa bodies) say pray both on the way before midnight; the four schools still count Isha as on time until Fajr when there is a need. Never let Fajr come without praying them. Prayed Maghrib before reaching Muzdalifah? For the majority it is valid; the Hanafis say it must be prayed again at Muzdalifah before Fajr.

Do you see the black stone in the corner of the Kaaba? The Prophet ﷺ told us it came down from Paradise, and that it was once whiter than milk. Before Muhammad ﷺ became a prophet, the people of Makkah rebuilt the Kaaba's walls. When it was time to put the Black Stone back, every tribe wanted the honour. They argued and argued and nearly started a fight! Then they agreed: the next man to walk in would decide. In walked Muhammad ﷺ — and everyone was happy, because they all called him al-Amin, the Trustworthy. He spread a cloth on the ground, put the Stone on it, and asked one man from every tribe to hold an edge. Together they lifted it — and he set the Stone in place with his own hands. Nobody fought. Being fair and trustworthy fixed everything.

Drink water often through the day, even when you are not thirsty. Water is best; avoid sugary and caffeinated drinks. If you have been sweating heavily, or feel weak or dizzy, oral rehydration salts or an isotonic drink help replace the salt you lose in sweat. Keep a filled bottle with you at Arafah, in Mina, at Muzdalifah and on the walk to the Jamarat. If a doctor limits how much you drink (for example for heart or kidney disease), ask them before you travel how to manage in the heat.

Drink water, charge your phone, put tomorrow's essentials (ihram spare, umbrella, dua list) in your day-bag. Go to bed early. In the morning, after Fajr and sunrise, move to Arafah with your group saying the talbiyah and the takbir.

Each jamrah is a basin with a wall standing in its middle. The Ministry of Hajj's guide says: throw seven pebbles, one at a time, and say "Allahu akbar" with each; aim at the wall in front of you so that the pebble lands in the basin; come from the least crowded side, and take care not to hit anyone. False — "I stood here, and all of Arafah is a place of standing." Sitting in your tent inside the boundary counts in full; climbing the hill is not a rite.

False — "Our Lord, do not hold us to account for what we forget or err in" (Quran {1}). There is no sin — learn, correct, continue. But most schools still require a fidyah for some slips (e.g. shaving or clipping nails), and most hold intercourse invalidates it even if forgotten — ask a scholar.
False — "Tawaf around the House is like salah, except that you speak in it; so whoever speaks, let him speak only good." (Tirmidhi {1})
False — "There are angels at the entrances of Madinah: neither plague nor the Dajjal can enter it." (Bukhari {1})
False — "all of Arafat is a place of standing" (Ibn Majah {1}); only the hollow of Uranah lies outside it. Sitting in the tent counts in full.
False — "except the menstruating women, who were excused" (Bukhari {1}). Tawaf al-ifadah, however, must still be done once she is pure.
False — Hajj adds Arafat, Muzdalifah, Mina and the fixed days of Dhul-Hijjah; Umrah is ihram, tawaf, sa'i and halq.
False — Jeddah lies inside the miqat boundaries for most routes, so ihram must be assumed before the plane crosses the miqat.

False — a child's Hajj is valid: when a woman held up a child and asked "Is there Hajj for this one?", the Prophet ﷺ said "Yes, and you will have a reward." But the scholars agree he must perform it again after puberty to fulfil the obligation.
False — beloved and highly virtuous (one of the three mosques worth travelling to — Bukhari {1}), but not part of the rites of Umrah or Hajj, and it needs no ihram.
False — both are sunnah for men in the arrival tawaf (Hanafis and Shafi'is: also in a later tawaf followed by sa'i); leaving them affects nothing.
False — no dua is prescribed per round. Only "Rabbana atina…" between the Yamani corner and Black Stone is sunnah.

False — tawaf al-ifadah is a pillar. "Would she delay us?" he asked about Safiyyah, until told she had already done it. She waits until she is pure; if her travel truly cannot wait, she asks a scholar before leaving. Only the farewell is waived.
False — the light jog there is for men; women walk throughout.
False — the opposite: the niqab is specifically not worn in ihram, and in the majority view gloves are not either (Bukhari {1}). Ordinary modest dress applies.
False — the requirement is an izar and rida not tailored to the body (a hem or seam is fine); clean is expected, white is recommended, and new is not required. Spares and washing are fine.
False — they first faced Jerusalem; the qibla changed mid-prayer (~{1} AH) — Quran {2}, commemorated at Masjid al-Qiblatayn.

Five stations: Makkah (in al-Rusaifah), Jeddah (al-Sulaymaniyah), King Abdulaziz International Airport (linked to Terminal {1}), King Abdullah Economic City, and Madinah (in Knowledge Economic City). The Makkah and Madinah stations are not next to the Harams: in a straight line they are about {2} km from the Ka'bah and about {3} km from the Prophet's Mosque, so plan a taxi or bus for the last part.

Five stations: Makkah (in al-Rusaifah), Jeddah (al-Sulaymaniyah), King Abdulaziz International Airport (linked to Terminal {1}), King Abdullah Economic City, and Madinah (in Knowledge Economic City). The Makkah and Madinah stations are not next to the Harams: in a straight line they are about {2} km from the Ka'bah and about {3} km from the Prophet's Mosque, so plan a taxi or bus for the last part. Official {4} journey times: about {5} minutes from the airport to Makkah, about {6} hour {7} minutes from the airport to Madinah, and about {8}¼ hours from Makkah to Madinah. Some trains take longer, so check the time of your own train, and book only on the official Haramain website or app. Going from Madinah to Makkah for Umrah or Hajj? The train does not stop at the miqat. Put on ihram before boarding, and make the intention before the train passes the miqat.
Flights & hotels confirmed — the dates cover {1}–{2} Dhul Hijjah
Follow it if you can — if the order changes, the schools differ on what is owed
Follow it if you can. If the group's schedule or the crowds change the order, nothing is lost — the Prophet ﷺ was asked about every variation that day and answered "no harm".

For about {1} months in Madinah the Muslims prayed towards Jerusalem, while the Prophet ﷺ longed for the Kaaba. Then mid-prayer the revelation came: <1>"Turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram"</1> (Quran {2}) — and the congregation turned as one. Masjid al-Qiblatayn ("the mosque of the two qiblas") in Madinah marks that moment.
For medical advice by phone, the Ministry of Health line {1} answers {2} hours a day (in the {3} Hajj season, in seven languages).

For the majority, the talbiyah continues from the miqat until you start your tawaf. Malikis stop it on entering the Haram (or, if ihram was from Tan'eem, on seeing the Kaaba) — if that is your school, your practice is sound.
For the majority, when does the Hajj pilgrim stop the talbiyah?

For the {1} season the Ministry of Hajj and Umrah set these dates: {2} {H1} {3} ({4} {M1} {5}) is the last day for issuing Umrah visas, {6} {H2} ({7} {M2} {8}) is the last day for Umrah pilgrims to enter the Kingdom, and {9} {H3} ({10} {M3} {11}) is the last day to leave. For whatever it is drunk for

Forgetfulness is excused — "Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or err" (Quran {1}). A man came to the Prophet ﷺ at Ji'ranah in a perfumed cloak; he was told to wash off the perfume and take the cloak off — nothing more (Bukhari {2}). Stop the act, remove the cause, carry on. Scholars differ on the fidyah: for perfume or clothing used through genuine forgetfulness or ignorance the Shafi'is and Hanbalis say nothing is due (this hadith is their evidence), while the Hanafis and Malikis generally still require one, and most scholars require one for cutting hair or nails, or hunting, even by mistake — ask a scholar.
Forgetting the talbiyah for a whole day

Forgot it or left it for later? Do it whenever you remember, even days later — it does not need ihram or a new tawaf, only to come after a tawaf you have already done (Malikis: do the sa'i straight after the tawaf; after a long gap repeat the tawaf first). Never done at all? It is a pillar for the majority (a wajib with a dam for Hanafis), so the Hajj stays incomplete until it is done. Tell your group leader / ask a scholar.
Forgot the ghusl or the perfume? Nothing is owed — both are sunnah. Just make the intention and carry on. If in doubt, tell your group leader or ask a scholar.

Forgot to cut? Cut now. Your ordinary clothes were never a problem — women wear them in ihram — and the delay itself owes nothing if you cut by the {1}th. If you did something else forbidden before cutting (perfume, cutting nails, niqab or gloves): Shafi'is and Hanbalis excuse perfume used forgetfully but not cutting nails; Hanafis require the fidyah regardless; Malikis owe nothing once you had stoned (the stoning alone opens their first tahallul); many contemporary scholars excuse all forgetting (Bukhari {2}) — a fast of {3} days, feeding {4} poor, or a sheep (Quran {5}; the amounts are from Bukhari {6}). Left Makkah without cutting? Cut as soon as you remember. Hanafis and Malikis say a dam is owed; Shafi'is and Hanbalis say nothing is owed for the delay. Tell your group leader / ask a scholar.
Forgotten PIN = lost documents. There is no reset — that is the point.

Found out later that a pebble was certainly missed? The schools differ. According to al-Mughni, Imam Ahmad's apparent view is that nothing is owed for one or two pebbles. The evidence given is Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (RA): coming back from the Hajj with the Prophet ﷺ, some said "I threw seven" and others "six", and none faulted the other (al-Nasa'i {1}; al-Albani: chain sahih; Zubair Ali Zai: da'if). Ibn Baz also excused a doubt about a single pebble. The Malikis owe a dam even for one pebble; the Shafi'is a dam for three, and a mudd of food for each pebble below that; the Hanafis half a sa' of food for each pebble, up to the value of a dam (al-Mughni). While the days of stoning last it can still be made up, and the order of the jamarat matters, so tell your group leader / ask a scholar.
Four: Hudaybiyyah, al-Qada, al-Ji'ranah, and the one with his Hajj (Bukhari {1}, {2}).

units.k: Groups are given set times for the Jamarat: keep to yours. The Ministry of Hajj and Umrah asks pilgrims to follow the official schedules to cut the risk of heat exhaustion and sunstroke. A later time costs you nothing: on the {1}th, {2}th and {3}th the stoning time starts after midday (about {4} pm in Mina in mid-{M1} {5}) and lasts until sunset (about {6} pm), and most scholars allow the night for those who could not stone by day (the Hanbali school: the next day after midday). On the {7}th the Prophet ﷺ stoned Jamrat al-Aqabah in the forenoon, and on the later days after midday (Muslim {8}). Take water and an umbrella, and get back into the shade straight after.

Hajj was legislated with the weak in mind: "the jihad of the elderly, the young, the weak and women is Hajj and Umrah" (Nasai {1}). Use what is permitted, without guilt.

Hajj {1} falls in mid-{M1} {2}. By the Umm al-Qura calendar, {3} Dhul Hijjah is {D1} {4} {M2} and the Day of Arafah is {D2} {5} {M3}; the official announcement can move this by a day. In Makkah the average May high is about {6}°C, and {7}°C has been recorded in May. The Saudi Ministry of Hajj and Umrah lists where heatstroke is common: tawaf at noon, sa'i when it is crowded and hot, Arafah at noon, and Mina, especially the slaughter areas and the Jamarat, because of the long walk and the crowding at the stoning. He repeated the same praise and dua on each hill (Muslim {1}) — persistence in dua is the lesson of sa'i.
He stands at Muzdalifah instead, which counts for Arafah
He stayed nine years in Madinah without performing Hajj, then announced it in the tenth year — his only Hajj after the Hijrah.

He stoned on the {1}th in the forenoon, and afterwards "when the sun had declined." Ibn Umar: "We used to wait till the sun declined." Whether you may stone after sunset differs: Hanafis and Shafi'is allow it, and the Saudi fatwa bodies follow this; the Hanbali school moves it to the next day after midday — follow your group.
He told them to leave it out
He touched the Yamani corner (Bukhari {1}) — no sound report has him kissing it — and recited this dua between the two corners (Abu Dawud {2}).

He ﷺ "kept reciting the talbiyah till he did the rami of Jamrat al-Aqabah" (Bukhari {1}). Some continue to the last pebble. Malikis stop it on arriving at Arafah after midday on the {2}th — if that is your school, your practice is sound.

He ﷺ "kept reciting the talbiyah till he did the rami of Jamrat al-Aqabah." Stopping at tawaf is the rule of Umrah, not Hajj. Some stop at the last pebble; Malikis stop on reaching Arafah after midday on the {1}th — if that is your school, your practice is sound.
He ﷺ "offered Maghrib and Isha together at al-Muzdalifah" (Bukhari {1}), with one adhan and two iqamahs and no sunnah prayers between them (Muslim {2}; Bukhari {3}).

He ﷺ lay down until dawn, prayed Fajr early, then stood at al-Mash'ar al-Haram making takbir, tahlil and dua "until the sky became very bright", and left before sunrise (Muslim {1}). Allah says: "remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram" (Quran {2}).

He ﷺ prayed Dhuhr and Asr together at Dhuhr time with one adhan and two iqamahs (Jabir, Muslim {1}), shortened to two rakahs each. Salim told al-Hajjaj, and Ibn Umar (RA) confirmed it: "if you want to follow the sunnah, pray early, just after midday, on the Day of Arafah" (Bukhari {2}).
He ﷺ spent the nights of tashriq in Mina (Aishah, Abu Dawud {1}) and permitted only those with a duty elsewhere to miss them (Bukhari {2}).
He ﷺ stayed "until the sun had set" and then departed (Muslim {1}), moving calmly, holding his camel back, telling the people: "calmness, calmness" (Muslim {2}).
He ﷺ stayed in Mina until the sun rose on the {1}th, then moved to Arafah (Muslim {2}).

He ﷺ stoned Jamrat al-Aqabah on the Day of Nahr in the forenoon, seven pebbles, saying Allahu akbar with each (Tirmidhi {1}, Bukhari {2}), and stopped the talbiyah with it (Bukhari {3}). After Aqabah he did not stop for dua (Bukhari {4}).
He ﷺ stoned, then slaughtered, then shaved, then went to the House — and when people did it in another order he said "do it, no harm" (Bukhari {1}, {2}).
Head out with wudu — the Haram fills early. May it be accepted.
Healthy, and only worried about the crowd? Go at a quieter time, such as the night (allowed by most scholars; the Hanbali school: the next day after midday), rather than delegate (Ibn Baz).

Heat is hardest on older people and on anyone with heart disease, diabetes, kidney or lung conditions, and some medicines add to the risk. Confusion is one of the signs of heatstroke, so the person may not ask for help: check on your companions through the day. See a doctor before you travel. Tell your group leader or group doctor early if anyone feels unwell; in the {1} season the Ministry of Health equipped field units near the holy sites with beds for heat exhaustion.

If standing in the crowds at dawn is beyond you — age, illness, pregnancy, small children, or you are the one escorting them — leave once the moon has set (on this night between about {1} and {2} am, in the last third of the night; Shafi'is and Hanbalis already allow leaving after midnight) and go to Mina. Leaving Muzdalifah after moonset is agreed for the weak; this is a concession the Prophet ﷺ gave, using it is not a shortcoming, and nothing is owed. The time of the stoning differs: Shafi'is and Hanbalis allow it from after midnight (Asma stoned before Fajr, Bukhari {3}); Hanafis and Malikis hold it is valid only from Fajr. Follow your group's school; if unsure, wait for Fajr — it is valid for everyone.

If you are lost, show your Nusuk card to security staff, a scout or a Nusuk Care point. The Ministry calls the card the main way to identify you and get you help. Scouts run guidance points for lost pilgrims across Mina and walk them back to their camp.

If you are pure: {1} rounds in ordinary clothes, no sa'i, then leave as your last act. If your period (or postnatal bleeding) has started and you have already done tawaf al-ifadah: you owe nothing and may leave straight away — say your goodbyes to the House with dua from the courtyard or the gate, without entering the prayer hall. If you have NOT yet done tawaf al-ifadah, that is a different matter — see its step.

If you can, follow the time and say the takbir where you are: Imam Ahmad liked the person to be present if able, and Malik said the sick person says the takbir in his lodging at the time (al-Mughni; al-Muwatta).

If you can, go back to the miqat and enter ihram there. If not, enter ihram where you are, <1>complete your Umrah or Hajj — it is valid</1> — and ask a scholar afterwards about the dam (a sheep slaughtered in the Haram) that most scholars require for crossing the miqat without ihram. Do not abandon your Umrah or Hajj over this.

If you cut your hair or changed into ordinary clothes after the arrival tawaf by mistake, your ihram still stands — put the ihram back on, stop the act, and carry on. Whether a fidyah is owed differs: Shafi'is and Hanbalis excuse perfume and clothing done forgetfully or unknowingly, but not cutting hair or nails; Hanafis and Malikis require the fidyah regardless; some Hanbalis and many contemporary scholars say nothing is owed for anything done forgetfully or unknowingly (Bukhari {1} — a man in a perfumed cloak was simply told to remove it). The fidyah is a fast of {2} days, feeding {3} poor, or a sheep (Quran {4}; the amounts are from the hadith of Ka'b ibn Ujrah, Bukhari {5}). Tell your group leader / ask a scholar whether one applies to you.

If you did sa'i after your arrival tawaf, nothing more is needed and you are now in the second tahallul. If you did not, do it now, straight after tawaf al-ifadah: Safa dhikr, {1} laps, finish on Marwah.

If you did sa'i after your arrival tawaf, you are done — one sa'i covers both for a Qarin by the majority view, and you are now in the second tahallul. If you did not, do it now after tawaf al-ifadah. Hanafis hold that a Qarin performs two sa'is (one for Umrah, one for Hajj): if you follow that school or your group leader says so, do the second one — an extra sa'i never harms.

If you discover you spent the whole day outside the boundary (in Uranah), move inside now — any moment inside Arafah between Dhuhr of the {1}th (Hanbalis: from Fajr of the {2}th) and Fajr of the {3}th makes the wuquf valid (Malikis: it must include a moment after sunset, so stay inside until the sun has set). Tell your group leader / ask a scholar.
If you leave Makkah while still on your period, no farewell tawaf is owed (Bukhari {1}) — and for Umrah many scholars require none at all.
If you walk, the Ministry advises a sun umbrella and comfortable shoes.

If you were not inside Arafah at any moment between Dhuhr on the {1}th (Hanbalis: from Fajr of the {2}th) and Fajr on the {3}th, there is no Hajj this year: you exit by doing the rites of Umrah (tawaf, sa'i, cut the hair) and make the Hajj up another year — a hady is owed according to the majority (Hanafis: none), and the Hajj is still obligatory on you. Arrived after sunset but before Fajr? Your wuquf is valid (Tirmidhi {4}). Tell your group leader / ask a scholar before you do anything.

In the year the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was born, a king called Abrahah had a big idea — a bad one. He wanted people to come to his own building instead of the Kaaba, so he marched to Makkah with a huge army and a giant elephant to knock the Kaaba down. The people of Makkah were scared. They could not fight such an army, so they left the city and watched from the hills. But the Kaaba belongs to Allah — and Allah protects His House. When the army came close, the elephant sat down and would not move! Then the sky filled with flocks of little birds, each carrying tiny stones. The birds dropped the stones, and the mighty army was beaten. Allah tells this story in the Quran in a short surah called al-Fil — "The Elephant". Can you recite it?

units.k: Islam planned for you. <1>Muzdalifah:</1> leave after midnight with your carer — the Prophet ﷺ sent the weak of his family ahead (Bukhari {1}); nothing is owed. The time of the stoning then differs: Shafi'is and Hanbalis allow it from after midnight (Asma stoned before Fajr, Bukhari {2}); Hanafis and Malikis hold it is valid only from Fajr — follow your group's school, and if unsure wait for Fajr, which is valid for everyone. <2>Stoning:</2> appoint someone who has stoned for themselves to throw on your behalf (permitted by all four schools — Ibn Majah {3} has a weak chain, its meaning is accepted; Malikis add a dam for the one unable) — your group leader can arrange it; or go at night (allowed by most scholars), when the bridge is quieter. <3>Tawaf and sa'i:</3> wheelchairs are valid — the Prophet ﷺ performed tawaf mounted (Bukhari {4}); wheelchairs (free or rented at official points around the Haram) and electric carts (upper floors and roof) are available — ask the Haram staff. Illness is not a shortcoming in your Hajj. Tell your group leader / ask a scholar.

It counts and it is rewarded: a woman lifted up a child and asked, "Is there Hajj for this one?" — "Yes, and you will have a reward" (Sahih Muslim). A child's Hajj does not fulfil the obligatory Hajj of Islam: the scholars agree it must be performed again after puberty (at-Tirmidhi, after hadith {1}). A <1>discerning child</1> (roughly {2}+) makes his or her own intention and does the rites; for a <2>young child</2> the guardian makes the intention on their behalf, carries or leads them round, and keeps them from the ihram prohibitions as far as a parent reasonably can. Whether one tawaf counts for both carrier and child is disputed: the Hanafis, and scholars such as Ibn Baz and al-Sa'di, say it counts for both when intended for both, while many Shafi'i and Hanbali scholars say it counts for only one of you — a separate tawaf for each is the safer course if you can manage it (ask if unsure). Boys shave or trim; girls trim. Resting, feeding and nappy changes are fine — see "Can I rest?" above.

It does not have to hit the wall: the wall only marks the target. A pebble that lands in the basin counts even if it bounces out again (Ibn Baz; Ibn Uthaymin; al-Fawzan). One that falls short does not count (al-Mughni). One that hits something hard or someone's clothing and then drops into the basin counts (al-Mughni; the Malikis likewise, Mukhtasar Khalil).

Long ago, Allah showed Prophet Ibrahim the place of His House and told him: keep it pure for those who come to worship. Then Allah told him: "Call the people to Hajj — they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel, from every distant road." Look around you now — people from every country and every colour, the men all in the same two white cloths. Every one of them is part of that promise. So are you!

Look around — thousands of people, and the men are all wearing the same two plain white cloths! No shirts, no fancy jackets, no trainers. That is called ihram. The Prophet ﷺ taught that a pilgrim leaves his everyday clothes behind, and he told us to wear white clothes and said they are among the best. Why does everyone dress the same? Because in front of Allah, a king and a street cleaner, a footballer and a farmer, a rich man and a poor man are exactly the same. Nobody can tell who is important — only Allah knows what is in our hearts. Women wear their ordinary modest clothes, and they are pilgrims too. Everyone says the same words — Labbayk Allahumma labbayk, "Here I am, O Allah!" — and everyone walks around the same Kaaba. One family, one Lord.

Men in ihram must not cover the head. The Prophet ﷺ forbade the man in ihram the turban and the hooded cloak (Bukhari {1}), and scholars agree this rules out a cap, hat or ghutra, or a towel or cloth laid on the head. Shade that does not touch the head is different.

Men in ihram must not cover the head. The Prophet ﷺ forbade the man in ihram the turban and the hooded cloak (Bukhari {1}), and scholars agree this rules out a cap, hat or ghutra, or a towel or cloth laid on the head. Shade that does not touch the head is different. Tents, buildings and trees: allowed by consensus. On the Day of Arafah the Prophet ﷺ rested in a tent pitched for him at Namirah (Muslim {2}). A hand-held umbrella: allowed by most scholars (the Hanafis, the Shafi'is, one narration from Imam Ahmad, and some Maliki authorities such as Khalil). When the Prophet ﷺ stoned Jamrat al-Aqabah, Usamah and Bilal (RA) were with him: one led his camel and the other held up a cloth over his head to shade him from the heat (Muslim {3}). Some jurists disliked or forbade it, but there is no consensus against it. Umbrella hats held on by a band round the head: better avoided. Most schools forbid tying a band round the head in ihram; Egypt's Dar al-Ifta allows such a hat only when nothing else is available, with a small charity if it is worn for a whole day, and advises a hand-held umbrella instead. Women cover their heads as usual, and may use an umbrella.

The Rawdah is a free Nusuk permit; the Black Stone is reached by patience or pointed to from afar, as the Prophet ﷺ did (Bukhari {1}); there is no private tawaf. Paying touts funds harassment of pilgrims and usually buys nothing.

Missed a whole day? Stone it the next day after midday, in order: the missed day's three first (only Aqabah if it was the {1}th), then that day's. Shafi'is and Hanbalis: nothing more is owed. Hanafis and Malikis: a dam for the delay (Hanafis: nothing for the {2}th if you stone before Fajr of the {3}th).

Missed after midday and left? Stone before sunset if you can get back; after sunset of the {1}th the days of stoning are over and a dam is owed for a day's stoning left undone (for a pebble or two the schools differ). Unable? Delegate (permitted by all four schools — Ibn Majah {2} has a weak chain, its meaning is accepted; Malikis add a dam for the one unable). Tell your group leader / ask a scholar.

Missed or done before midday? Repeat after midday, or stone tomorrow in order (the {1}th's three, then the {2}th's) — the stoning is made up; Shafi'is and Hanbalis: nothing more is owed, Hanafis and Malikis: a dam for the delay. If the {3}th passes with it undone, a dam is owed by all. Unable? Delegate (permitted by all four schools — Ibn Majah {4} has a weak chain, its meaning is accepted; Malikis add a dam for the one unable). Tell your group leader / ask a scholar.

Missed today? Stone it tomorrow before that day's three, in order: today's three first, then tomorrow's — the stoning is made up. Shafi'is and Hanbalis: nothing more is owed; Hanafis and Malikis: a dam is owed for the delay. Stoned before midday? The majority count it as not done — repeat it after midday (Hanafis allow before midday only on the {1}th; a few contemporary scholars permit it on the {2}th for the weak in severe crowding — ask before relying on it). Unable to go? Delegate to someone who has stoned for themselves (permitted by all four schools — Ibn Majah {3} has a weak chain, its meaning is accepted; Malikis add a dam for the one unable). If the {4}th passes with any day undone, a dam is owed by all. Tell your group leader / ask a scholar.

Missed with no excuse? For a single night the schools differ: the Malikis owe a dam, as do the Hanbalis in their relied-upon view (another Hanbali view: a mudd of food), the Shafi'is a mudd of food, the Hanafis nothing (they count the nights as sunnah); missing all the nights owes a dam for the majority. Valid excuses remove it. Tell your group leader / ask a scholar.

Missed with no excuse? For this night alone the schools differ: the Malikis owe a dam, as do the Hanbalis in their relied-upon view (another Hanbali view: a mudd of food), the Shafi'is a mudd of food, the Hanafis nothing; missing all the nights owes a dam for the majority — see the night of the {1}th. Excuses (illness, caring, no space) remove it. Tell your group leader / ask a scholar.

Shortening is for travellers: Malikis shorten in Mina and Arafah regardless (as do many Saudi scholars today); Hanafis ({1}+ days in Makkah before the {2}th) count you a resident and pray four rakahs here; Shafi'is count you a resident after {3} full days in Makkah (not counting the days of arrival and departure), but let you shorten from the moment you leave for Mina if you will set off for home after the rites without another {4} full days in Makkah (al-Majmu' {5}/{6}); Hanbalis shorten unless you will stay on in Makkah for more than {7} days after the Hajj — ask your group leader which your group follows. Most scholars hold tawaf is not valid without wudu, so make it before you enter. If it breaks mid-tawaf, renew it: the Hanafi and Shafi'i schools let you continue from where you stopped; the Maliki and Hanbali schools say restart the tawaf, which is the safer course. units.k: Muzdalifah and Mina: where they begin and end

Muzdalifah is wide ("all of Muzdalifah is a place of standing" — Abu Dawud {1}), but check the boundary signs where your bus stops; the valley of Muhassir is outside it. Pray as soon as you arrive — Maghrib in full, Isha shortened (four rakahs if your school counts you a resident of Makkah — see the {2}th; in the relied-upon Shafi'i view such a resident also prays the two each at its own time), no nafl after. If you fear you will arrive only after midnight, many scholars (including the Saudi fatwa bodies) say pray both on the way before midnight; the four schools still count Isha as on time until Fajr when there is a need. Never let Fajr come without praying them.

Muzdalifah lies between Arafah and Mina. Its eastern edge, towards Arafah, is the pass between the two mountains of al-Ma'zimayn. Its western edge is the eastern bank of Wadi Muhassir, the valley that separates it from Mina; the valley itself is not part of Muzdalifah. Mina runs west from Wadi Muhassir up to Jamrat al-Aqabah. The Prophet ﷺ said: "I stood here, and all of Jam' (Muzdalifah) is a place of standing" (Muslim {1}). Reports in the Muwatta and Ibn Majah tell pilgrims to keep out of the hollow of Muhassir. Where your bus stops, look for the boundary signs, and ask your group leader if you are unsure.
Muzdalifah to the Jamarat: about {1} km from the middle of Muzdalifah; less from its Mina side, more from its Arafah side. {2} to {3} hours.

No one fasts on the Day of Eid (Bukhari {1}). The days of tashriq, the {2}th, {3}th and {4}th, are "days of eating, drinking and remembrance of Allah" (Muslim {5}). Fasting them was allowed only for the pilgrim who could not afford a hady (Bukhari {6}, {7}), and even that is disputed: the Malikis, the Hanbalis and al-Shafi'i's old view allow that pilgrim to fast them; the Hanafis and the relied-upon Shafi'i view do not. On the journey you may fast or not. The Prophet ﷺ told a Companion, "Fast if you wish, and do not fast if you wish" (Bukhari {1}), and called it "a concession from Allah: whoever takes it has done well, and whoever prefers to fast has no sin" (Muslim {2}). Any day you do not fast is made up later. Once you are staying in Makkah or Madinah, scholars differ. Most (the Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools) count you a resident, who must fast, once you intend to stay in one city for about four days or more: the Shafi'is and Malikis count four full days, not counting the days you arrive and leave; the Hanbalis, more than four days. The Hanafi school sets the line at an intended stay of {3} days or more. Other scholars hold that the concession lasts as long as you are travelling, however long you stay. Ask a scholar you trust, or your group's guide, which view to follow.

Once, Prophet Ibrahim brought his wife Hajar and their baby Isma'il to this valley. There was no water, no crops, no people — just sand and two little hills. Allah had told him to leave them here. Hajar asked, "Did Allah tell you to do this?" Ibrahim said yes. Hajar said, "Then Allah will not leave us alone." Soon the water ran out and the baby cried. Hajar climbed the hill of Safa to look for help — nothing. She ran to the hill of Marwah — nothing. Seven times she ran between the two hills! Then she heard a sound. Next to her baby, water was bubbling up out of the ground — Zamzam! Allah had sent it. When we walk seven times between Safa and Marwah, we are remembering brave Hajar and how she trusted Allah. And the Zamzam you drink today is that very same water.

Pilgrims at Mina do not hold the Eid prayer. On the Day of Nahr the Prophet ﷺ stoned Jamrat al-Aqabah, sacrificed and rode on to the House (Jabir, Muslim {1}), and gave a sermon that day (Bukhari {2}, {3}); Eid fell during his Hajj and he did not pray it, as the Hanbali jurists point out. None of the four schools asks the pilgrim to hold it, to lighten a day full of rites: the Hanafis say it is not held at Mina; the Malikis, that it is not recommended for the pilgrim; the Hanbalis make settled residence a condition of the Eid prayer; the Shafi'is say the pilgrim does not pray it in congregation, but may pray it alone, and some of them call that better. Spend the morning on the stoning, the sacrifice, the shave and tawaf al-ifadah, with the takbir on your tongue.

Asked how the Prophet ﷺ washed his head in ihram, Abu Ayyub (RA) had water poured over his own head, passed his hands over it from front to back and said, "This is how I saw him do it" (Bukhari {1}). units.k: Prophet Ibrahim saw in a dream that Allah wanted him to sacrifice his son — most scholars say it was Isma'il. It was the hardest thing in the world. He asked his son, and his son said: "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, patient." They both obeyed — and Allah called out to Ibrahim that he had fulfilled the dream, and ransomed his son with a great sacrifice. On Eid al-Adha we sacrifice too, and Allah tells us what matters: "Their meat will not reach Allah, nor will their blood, but what reaches Him is your taqwa."

Signs: body temperature of {1}°C or more; hot, red skin that may be dry or still sweaty; fast heartbeat and fast breathing; confusion, odd behaviour, or seeing and hearing things that are not there; a seizure; collapse or loss of consciousness. What to do: call {2} first (or {3}, the Saudi Red Crescent). Then cool the person hard while you wait: move them to shade or air conditioning, remove outer clothing, pour or spray cool water over them, especially the head and neck, and fan them; put ice or cold packs on the neck and armpits if you have them. Do not try to make someone drink if they are confused, drowsy or unconscious. If they become unconscious, lay them on their side in the recovery position and check their breathing; start CPR if there is no sign of life. For medical advice by phone, the Ministry of Health line {4} answers {5} hours a day (in the {6} Hajj season, in seven languages).

Signs: headache; dizziness or fainting; heavy sweating with pale, clammy skin; nausea or vomiting; cramps; tiredness or weakness; intense thirst. What to do: get into shade or air conditioning. Loosen or remove extra clothing. Spray or sponge the skin with cool water, especially the head and neck, and fan it; cold packs wrapped in cloth on the neck or armpits help. Drink cold water, or oral rehydration salts mixed with water. Stay with the person: they should feel better within about {1} minutes. If they are not better by then, or they vomit, or they get worse, call {2}. Heat exhaustion can turn into heatstroke.

Stop the act, remove the cause, put the ihram back on and continue — the Hajj stands. <1>Forgetting or not knowing:</1> Shafi'is and Hanbalis excuse perfume and clothing but not cutting hair or nails; Hanafis and Malikis require the fidyah regardless; some Hanbalis and many contemporary scholars say nothing is owed (Bukhari {1} — a man in a perfumed cloak was simply told to remove it). A <2>deliberate</2> violation (perfume, cutting hair or nails, men covering the head or wearing stitched clothes) needs the fidyah by all once it reaches each school's threshold: fast three days, or feed six poor people, or slaughter a sheep (Quran {2}; the amounts are from the hadith of Ka'b ibn Ujrah, Bukhari {3}) — Hanafis give this choice only when there was an excuse; without one they require a sheep. Below the threshold less is owed — for hair, a mudd of food per hair under three hairs (Shafi'is and Hanbalis) or a charity under a quarter of the head (Hanafis). <3>Intimacy</3> is different: before the first tahallul (Hanafis: before Arafah) it spoils the Hajj — you still complete it and repeat it another year, and a camel (badanah) is owed (Malikis: a hady; Hanafis: a sheep). The Haram at {1}am is an experience you will never forget.
The Hijrah & the Conquest of Makkah
The House of Allah, qibla of the world, site of your tawaf. "The first House established for mankind" (Quran {1}); every prayer here is worth {2} (Ibn Majah {3}).
The Jamarat: order, where you aim, the building

The Kaaba has been rebuilt several times — by Quraysh in the Prophet's ﷺ youth (when funds ran short, they left out part of the original foundation, which is why the <1>Hijr Isma'il</1> semicircle stands outside the walls today). The Prophet ﷺ told Aishah: <2>"Do you not know that when your people rebuilt the Kaaba, they decreased it from the original foundations of Ibrahim?"</2> (Bukhari {1}). The black kiswah covering is renewed every year, embroidered with gold calligraphy — a tradition of honouring the House that is centuries old.
The Kaaba is described in the Quran as…
The Kaaba — the House of Allah that Prophet Ibrahim built with his son Isma'il!
The Ministry of Hajj advises saving these and carrying proof of them — roads and camps in Mina look very alike.
The Prophet ﷺ "kept on reciting the talbiyah till he did the rami of Jamrat al-Aqabah" (Bukhari {1}).
The Prophet ﷺ bathed before entering ihram (Tirmidhi {1}) — you meet Allah's House purified inside and out.

The Prophet ﷺ bathed before ihram (Tirmidhi {1}) and was perfumed by Aishah (RA) before assuming it (Bukhari {2}). On the {3}th his companions who had done Umrah assumed ihram for Hajj from where they were staying in Makkah (Muslim {4}, {5}).
The Prophet ﷺ entered ihram at Dhul-Hulayfah after praying there — beginning the journey with salah is his way.
The Prophet ﷺ had his tent pitched at Namirah on the day of Arafah, then addressed the people and prayed Dhuhr and Asr combined (Muslim {1}). One of the largest mosques in the world.
The Prophet ﷺ made dua on Safa and Marwah — pour out your heart.

The Prophet ﷺ ordered it as the last act before leaving (Bukhari {1}, Muslim). He ﷺ himself did it at night, after Isha and a short sleep at al-Muhassab, before setting out for Madinah (Anas, Bukhari {2}).

The Prophet ﷺ prayed Dhuhr to Fajr in Mina on the {1}th, and the four schools agree this stay is a sunnah — nothing is owed for missing it. Arafah and tawaf al-ifadah are pillars; the stoning is a wajib.

The Prophet ﷺ returned to Mina (Muslim {1}) and spent the nights of tashriq there (Aishah, Abu Dawud {2}); he exempted only the water-carriers of Zamzam and the herdsmen from the nights (Bukhari {3}, Abu Dawud {4}) — so for everyone else it is a duty (the majority view; Hanafis: a sunnah).
The Prophet ﷺ said about Uhud…

The Prophet ﷺ said the Black Stone <1>descended from Paradise whiter than milk, and the sins of the children of Adam blackened it</1> (Tirmidhi {1}). Years before prophethood, when Quraysh rebuilt the Kaaba, the tribes nearly fought over who would set the Stone in place. The young Muhammad ﷺ — already called al-Amin, the Trustworthy — laid it on a cloth so every tribe could lift a corner together, and he set it with his own hands.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Hajj is Arafah" (Tirmidhi {1}), and: "I stood here, and all of Arafah is a place of standing" (Muslim {2}). So make sure you are inside Arafah for the standing, and check with your eyes, not with a phone. Signboards mark Arafah's boundary; read them to see which side is Arafah. The valley of Uranah, on Arafah's western edge, is not part of Arafah, and the western (front) part of Masjid Namirah stands in it. The Ministry of Hajj advises staying in your camp, because Arafah's roads look alike and it is easy to get lost, and praying there rather than going to Masjid Namirah unless necessary, to avoid getting lost or heatstroke. If you are unsure, ask your group leader or an official.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Take suhoor, for there is blessing in suhoor" (Bukhari {1}). You may eat and drink until dawn, when the fast begins (Quran {2}). The Grand Mosque gives two adhans for Fajr: an earlier first call, then the Fajr adhan itself. In the Prophet's ﷺ time Bilal also called before dawn, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Eat and drink until Ibn Umm Maktum calls the adhan" (Bukhari {3}). When the app shows calculated prayer times (marked ±{4} min), Fajr can be a minute or two off the official timetable, so stop eating a few minutes early.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "The best of supplication is the supplication of the Day of Arafah, and the best of what I and the prophets before me have said is: la ilaha illallahu wahdahu la sharika lah…" (Tirmidhi {1}). Grade: al-Albani, hasan; al-Tirmidhi called it hasan gharib and noted that one narrator is not strong; Zubair Ali Zai, da'if. Malik reports a shorter wording as a mursal report (al-Muwatta).

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and hoping for reward will have his past sins forgiven" (Bukhari {1}). And: "The fasting person has two joys: one when he breaks his fast, and one when he meets his Lord" (Bukhari {2}).

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever gives a fasting person food to break his fast will have the same reward as him, without the fasting person's reward being reduced at all" (Tirmidhi {1}, which al-Tirmidhi called hasan sahih and al-Albani graded sahih). Inside the two Harams, iftar is served through an official programme: in {H1} {2} ({3}), donors booked iftar spreads on the website of the mosques' authority, paid through the Ehsan platform, and approved caterers served the meals. Look for the authority's announcement for {H2} {4}.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever prays at night in Ramadan out of faith and hoping for reward will have his past sins forgiven" (Bukhari {1}), and: "Whoever prays with the imam until he finishes, a whole night of prayer is written for him" (Tirmidhi {2}, which al-Tirmidhi called hasan sahih and al-Albani graded sahih). In the Grand Mosque, taraweeh is prayed in congregation after Isha. In the last ten nights a second congregational night prayer, tahajjud, is held late in the night. Times and imams are announced each year.

The Prophet ﷺ said: <1>"The jihad of the elderly, the young, the weak and women is Hajj and Umrah."</1> (Nasai {1}). And when Aishah (RA) asked if women have jihad, he said: "Jihad in which there is no fighting — Hajj and Umrah." (Ibn Majah {2}). Every drop of sweat in the mataf is counted.

The Prophet ﷺ said: <1>"Umrah to Umrah is an expiation for the sins committed between them, and the accepted Hajj has no reward except Paradise."</1> (Bukhari {1}). Whoever performs the pilgrimage without obscenity or wickedness "returns as the day his mother bore him" (Muslim {2}). You come home with a clean slate — guard it.

The Prophet ﷺ said: <1>"Whoever eats seven Ajwa dates in the morning will not be harmed that day by poison or magic."</1> (Bukhari {1}). He also made dua: "O Allah, bless Madinah with twice the blessings You gave Makkah." (Bukhari {2}). Bring Ajwa home as your gift.

The Prophet ﷺ said: <1>"Zamzam water is for whatever it is drunk for."</1> (Ibn Majah {1}) and called it "blessed — a food that nourishes" (Muslim {2}); another narration adds "and a cure for illness" (al-Tayalisi, al-Bazzar). Drink your fill, face the qibla, and ask Allah for exactly what you need — knowledge, cure, forgiveness.
The Prophet ﷺ sent her with her brother Abdur-Rahman to Tan'eem: "This Umrah is instead of your missed one." Today Masjid Aisha stands there.

The Prophet ﷺ sent the weak of his family ahead on the night of Muzdalifah (Bukhari {1}); Ibn Umar (RA) would send them ahead by night (Bukhari {2}); Asma (RA) left when the moon set and stoned the Jamrah before Fajr (Bukhari {3}).
The Prophet ﷺ visited every Saturday, walking or riding (Bukhari {1}) — make wudu at your hotel and go at least once.
The Prophet ﷺ was born there
The Prophet's ﷺ mosque, built with his own hands — one prayer here is better than a thousand elsewhere, except al-Masjid al-Haram (Bukhari {1}).
The Prophet's ﷺ own four Umrahs

The Quran gives the alternative itself: <1>fast three days during Hajj and seven when you return home — ten in all</1> (Quran {1}). Best the {2}th–{3}th (Shafi'i) or the {4}th–{5}th (Hanafi / Hanbali — the {6}th is allowed for the one who owes this fast; a pilgrim with nothing to make up does not fast Arafah). Missed them? Malikis and Hanbalis allow the days of tashriq (Bukhari {7}–{8}), as does al-Shafi'i's old view; the relied-upon Shafi'i view does not, so the three days are made up later; Hanafis say the hady is then owed instead. Many groups can also sponsor a voucher — ask. Tell your group leader / ask a scholar.
The Rawdah is described by the Prophet ﷺ as…

The Rawdah visit permit and the Umrah permit are <1>free on the Nusuk app</1>, and a Hajj permit comes only with a licensed Hajj package. Anyone selling you a "permit", "slot" or "VIP access" is selling you nothing. And in Saudi Arabia, collecting donations in streets and mosques is <2>illegal outside official platforms</2> — the Kingdom's official donation platform is <3><4>Ehsan (ehsan.sa)</4></3>. units.k: The famous fast of Arafah is for those not on Hajj. At Arafah the Prophet ﷺ did not fast: when people disagreed about it, Umm al-Fadl (RA) sent him a cup of milk and he drank it on his camel (Bukhari {1}; Muslim {2}). Maymunah (RA) reported the same, with the people watching (Bukhari {3}; Muslim {4}). Ibn Umar (RA) said that neither the Prophet ﷺ nor Abu Bakr, Umar or Uthman fasted it on Hajj (Tirmidhi {5}). At-Tirmidhi wrote that most scholars prefer that the pilgrim not fast at Arafah, to have strength for dua, though some did fast it (Tirmidhi {6}).

The hady is the sacrifice of Hajj. It is owed by a pilgrim doing Tamattu' or Qiran (Quran {1}) and is slaughtered within the Haram: "all of Mina is a place of sacrifice" (Abu Dawud {2}). A pilgrim doing Ifrad owes none. Cannot afford it? Fast three days during the Hajj and seven when you are home (Quran {3}). True — "it is a part of the House" (Tirmidhi {1}): the part next to the Kaaba wall, roughly six cubits deep, lay inside the original Kaaba (Muslim {2}), so pray close to the wall. A rare chance most pilgrims miss!

True — "…as the bellows removes the dross of iron, gold and silver." (Tirmidhi {1})

True — Allah warns against "deviation to wrongdoing" in the Haram (Quran {1}). Guard your tongue and gaze doubly.

True — Ibn Umar (RA): "Whoever is at Mina when the sun sets on the middle day of tashreeq must not leave until he has stoned the jamarat the next day." True — Sawdah (RA), a slow woman, asked and he allowed her to leave before the rush; Ibn Abbas was sent ahead with the weak of the family. The schools differ on the earliest time (Shafi'is and Hanbalis: after midnight) — follow your group.
True — a belt is not fitted "stitched clothing"; it is how you keep your passport and cash safe.

True — a pillar is never "too late": the Hajj is completed when it is done. With an excuse such as a period, nothing is owed. Delaying it without an excuse is discouraged, and some schools then owe a dam (Hanafis, once the days of sacrifice have passed; Malikis, once Dhul Hijjah ends).

True — after her Hajj, the Prophet ﷺ sent Aishah (RA) with her brother to Tan'eem for an Umrah (Bukhari {1}, {2}). Most scholars allow it; Malikis dislike more than one Umrah a year, and some (e.g. Ibn Taymiyyah) prefer extra tawaf instead.
True — continue from where you left off. "Allah intends for you ease" (Quran {1}).
True — crossing your miqat without ihram when intending Umrah requires returning to it, or else, for most scholars, a dam (a sheep slaughtered in the Haram).

True — he declared sacred what lies between its two lava plains, as Ibrahim declared Makkah sacred (Muslim {1}). Most scholars forbid hunting and cutting its trees, though its rules are lighter than Makkah's; Hanafis do not give it Makkah's rulings.
True — one direction is one lap; seven laps finish on Marwah.
True — tawaf is like prayer (Tirmidhi {1}); keep your wudu, and renew it if broken.
True — the Prophet ﷺ confirmed a child's pilgrimage counts (Muslim {1}); parents make intention for infants.
True — the Prophet ﷺ made dua for those who shave three times, and once for those who trim (Bukhari {1}, Muslim {2}).
True — the Prophet ﷺ sent the weak of his family ahead on the night of Muzdalifah (Bukhari {1}); Asma (RA) left when the moon had set (Bukhari {2}).

True — unlike Hajj, Umrah has no fixed date. (Ramadan carries a special reward.) Hanafis dislike it on {1}–{2} Dhul Hijjah, and Saudi authorities pause Umrah permits around the Hajj season — check Nusuk for your dates.
True — whoever performs it without obscenity or sin returns cleansed of sins (Bukhari {1}, Muslim {2}).

Yes, if you cannot do it yourself, or only with real hardship: illness, old age, pregnancy, blindness or weakness, or a mother with small children and no one to mind them. A guardian also stones for a small child. Delegation is permitted by all four schools (al-Mughni); the Malikis add that the one unable still owes a dam (al-Muwatta; Mukhtasar Khalil). The Companions stoned on behalf of the children (Ibn Majah {1}: weak chain, its meaning is accepted).

Yes, if you genuinely cannot go: illness, old age, pregnancy, disability, a small child, or real fear of the crush. Jabir (RA): "we recited the talbiyah on behalf of the children and stoned the pillars on their behalf" (agreed fiqh — Ibn Majah {1} has a weak chain, its meaning is accepted); scholars extend this to any adult unable to go (Malikis add a dam for the adult who is unable). Rules of thumb: the proxy should have <1>stoned for themselves first</1> that day (or throw yours jamarah by jamarah after their own); they say the takbir with each pebble as usual; you make dua where you are. Finding it merely tiring is not an excuse — most scholars allow the night hours for those who could not go in the day (the Hanbali school: the next day after midday), and the bridge is quieter then. Tell your group leader; most groups organise proxies for the elderly. Ask a scholar if you are unsure whether your reason counts.

You have not lost the Hajj. <1>Stone it the next day, in order:</1> yesterday's jamarat first (small→middle→Aqabah; only Aqabah if you missed the {1}th), then today's — all after midday. The stoning is made up: Shafi'is and Hanbalis say nothing more is owed; Hanafis and Malikis say a <2>dam</2> (a sheep, slaughtered and given to the poor of the Haram) is owed for the delay. If the {2}th passes with any stoning undone, a dam is owed by all. If you cannot physically go, <3>delegate</3> it to someone who has already stoned for themselves (permitted by all four schools — Ibn Majah {3} has a weak chain, its meaning is accepted; Malikis add a dam for the one unable). Tell your group leader / ask a scholar.

Your Hajj company moves you between the sites on a fixed plan, by bus or train, and some groups walk to the Jamarat. The Ministry of Hajj tells pilgrims to travel with their group by the designated transport, for example from Arafah to Muzdalifah, and in {1} it asked pilgrims not to walk between the sites at the restricted times. If your group's plan does include walking, these are rough guides at a steady {2} to {3} km an hour. Walking routes are longer than these distances, and crowds and heat slow you down, so allow more time: - Haram to the Jamarat: about {4} km in a straight line; camps at the far (Muzdalifah) end of Mina are about {5} km or more. {6} to {7} hours. - Mina to Arafah: about {8} km, more between camps far apart. {9} to {10} hours or more. - Muzdalifah to the Jamarat: about {11} km from the middle of Muzdalifah; less from its Mina side, more from its Arafah side. {12} to {13} hours. - Arafah to Muzdalifah: about {14} to {15} km. {16} to {17}½ hours. If you walk, the Ministry advises a sun umbrella and comfortable shoes.

Your Hajj is intact. Arafah, Muzdalifah, the stoning, the trim — all valid without purity. Only tawaf al-ifadah (and the sa'i after it) waits: carry on with every other rite, and after the stoning and the trim on the {1}th stay in the first tahallul; keep up the dhikr and dua from the courtyards, and do ghusl, tawaf and sa'i when you are pure — even on the {2}th or later. Aishah (RA), whose period came before her tawaf, was told: "Do all that the pilgrims do, except the tawaf of the House until you are pure" (Bukhari {3}, {4}). <1>The farewell tawaf is waived</1> for you if you are still on your period when you leave (Bukhari {5}). If the group's flight comes before purity, scholars differ — some permit tawaf with precautions in genuine necessity; do not decide alone at the airport: tell your group leader / ask a scholar now, not on the last day.
Your Hajj is invalid and must be repeated

Your Umrah needs a free Umrah permit (a date-and-time slot) in the Nusuk app, in Ramadan as at any time of year. Nusuk allows one active permit at a time: you can book another once it expires, or cancel it before its start time. Praying in the Grand Mosque needs no permit. In past Ramadans the Ministry of Hajj and Umrah has limited repeat Umrahs to ease crowding: in {1} it said each person could perform Umrah only once in Ramadan, in {2} it said no permit would be issued for a second Umrah in Ramadan, and in {3} it encouraged pilgrims to perform Umrah only once in the last ten days. Check Nusuk for the rule in {H1} {4}.

Your Umrah sa'i was for the Umrah; this one is for the Hajj. Straight after tawaf al-ifadah, in ordinary clothes: the same Safa dhikr, {1} laps, finish on Marwah. Use the sa'i counter. With tawaf and sa'i done you are in the second tahallul — everything is allowed.

Your group decides how and when you go. Some groups take the Mashaer train, whose last station is on the {1}th level of the Jamarat facility, and then walk a short way. Others go by buses set aside for particular groups, or on foot; if you walk, the Ministry advises a sun umbrella and comfortable shoes. Golf carts carry the elderly and those who find walking hard, especially up to the Jamarat Bridge. Go at your group's stoning time. In {2} ({3}) the Ministry's instructions to Hajj companies said pilgrims going to the stoning should not bring children or luggage, or use wheelchairs; check this season's rules with your company. If you are elderly, weak, ill or pregnant, or fear harm, you may appoint another pilgrim to stone for you (tawkil). Your proxy stones for himself first, then for you.
